summary:
Lembranza is an interactive website that tells the stories of NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars, written for school-age space enthusiasts. Seventeen mission stories (eight lunar, nine Martian) run from Apollo landers and Viking to Perseverance, each labeled still working, mission complete, crashed on purpose, or lost. A Field Guide with a quiz, glossary and classroom activities, a Discoveries section and a clue-based Mission Games page turn the stories into learning.

It answers the challenge directly: it introduces each machine, its purpose and its current condition, then shows the science it made possible, from the Moon drifting away from Earth to ancient water on Mars.

It matters because “abandoned” does not mean “worthless.” These machines record human curiosity, and their data still informs Artemis and future Mars missions. A retro-futuristic design, short readable text and reduced-motion support make that story engaging and accessible.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Beyond our sky, machines are sitting very still. There are footprints on the Moon that no wind will ever erase, and rovers resting in Martian dust beneath the last sunset they saw. Abandoned. Not Forgotten. is a website that walks up to each of them and lets it tell its story.

Seventeen stories carry the reader across two worlds, eight on the Moon and nine on Mars, from Apollo’s landers and lunar rovers to Viking, Opportunity, Ingenuity and Perseverance. Every machine wears a status (still working, mission complete, crashed on purpose, lost), so a child can see at a glance how its journey ended. Around the stories sit a Field Guide with a quiz, a glossary and classroom activities, a Discoveries page that links each machine to the science it unlocked, and a clue-based game where players name the mission behind the hint.

What are its benefits?

It turns space history from a list of dates into a cast of characters. It is free, light enough for a school’s slow Wi-Fi, readable on a phone, usable by keyboard, and gentle on anyone sensitive to motion. Teachers receive activities, and curious kids receive a reason to keep scrolling.

What impact do we intend?

I want one word to change its meaning: “Abandoned”. It should stop sounding like thrown away and start sounding like parked on another world, still teaching. A mirror left on the Moon in 1969 still answers laser beams today, and old data still guides the missions yet to fly. If a child leaves knowing that, and perhaps dreams of naming the next rover, the machines were not abandoned at all.

What tools, languages and software did we use?

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with no frameworks standing between the reader and the story. A canvas draws the stars. Layered CSS adds nebulae, planets and a perspective grid. Typography comes from Google Fonts (Orbitron, Michroma, Syncopate, Silkscreen, DM Sans and DM Mono). We built in VS Code, versioned on GitHub, and researched from NASA Science, JPL, the NASA Image and Video Library and LROC. I drafted and organised content, and an AI coding assistant helped implement the code, with the myself directing and reviewing the work. The only hardware was a laptop and a browser.

How is it creative?

It dresses 1960s and 1970s hardware in the cockpit of an imagined 1980s future: a time capsule wearing a time machine’s interface, with neon light, notched panels and arcade lettering. As you scroll, planets drift into view, swell as if approaching, then dissolve behind you, like the residue every mission leaves. The machines are treated as characters with biographies, so I tell their stories instead of listing their specifications.

What factors did we consider?

  • Truth. Facts come from NASA and JPL sources, and anything we could not confirm was flagged or left out.
  • Audience. I used short sentences and plain words, with a glossary for the rest.
  • Accessibility. I kept contrast high, keyboard focus visible and motion optional, including a reduced-motion setting.
  • Restraint. Beauty must never block reading.
  • Performance. The site stays lightweight, with no heavy dependencies.
  • Respect. I credit imagery from NASA’s public media, make no claim of NASA endorsement, and disclose our use of AI.
  • Honesty. Lost missions and ended journeys belong in the story alongside the triumphs.
